items.title: A missed report deadline
items.situation: You work in the marketing department of a medium-sized firm. Your manager, Ms Grant, asked you to finish a sales report by nine o'clock this morning for a meeting with senior directors. You underestimated how long the figures would take to check, and the report is still not ready. The meeting starts in an hour, and Ms Grant has just walked over to your desk to collect it. What would you say to Ms Grant?
points: Take responsibility straight away and apologise
Explain honestly what went wrong without long excuses
Say exactly what is ready now and when the rest will be
Offer something useful for the meeting, such as a summary of key figures

items.title: Asking for flexible hours
items.situation: You have worked as an accounts assistant for two years and have a good record. You have just enrolled in an evening course at a local college, which starts at half past five on Tuesdays and Thursdays, but your working day ends at half past five. You would like to start and finish an hour earlier on those two days. You have arranged a short meeting with your supervisor, Mr Harper. What would you say to Mr Harper?
points: Explain the course and how it relates to your work if possible
Make a precise request: which days and which hours
Reassure him that your work will not suffer
Offer to review the arrangement after a trial period

items.title: Turning down an extra project
items.situation: Your team leader, Daniel, has asked you to lead a new customer survey project starting next week. You are already managing two large projects with tight deadlines, and you have been working late most evenings to keep up. You know that taking on a third project would mean doing all three badly. Daniel has asked you to come to his office to discuss it. What would you say to Daniel?
points: Thank him for trusting you with the project
Explain your current workload with specific examples
Decline clearly but constructively
Suggest an alternative, such as a later start or a colleague who could lead it

items.title: A colleague's loud phone calls
items.situation: You share an open-plan office with a friendly colleague called Chris. For the past few weeks, Chris has been taking long personal phone calls on speakerphone at his desk, sometimes for half an hour at a time. You find it very hard to concentrate, especially when you are writing reports, and two other colleagues have mentioned it to you as well. You get on well with Chris and do not want to upset him. What would you say to Chris?
points: Keep a friendly tone that suits the relationship
Describe the problem and its effect on your work
Avoid sounding as if others are ganging up on him
Suggest a simple solution, such as headphones or a meeting room

items.title: A friend's first job interview
items.situation: Your friend Aisha has just been invited to her first job interview, for a graduate role at an engineering company. The interview is next week, and she has admitted she has done nothing to prepare because she does not know where to start. She is also worried because she has no work experience apart from a summer job in a cafe. She has asked for your help. What advice would you give Aisha?
points: Encourage her and show confidence in her
Suggest researching the company and the role
Advise preparing examples, including from the cafe job
Mention practical details such as questions to ask and arriving early

items.title: Negotiating a job offer
items.situation: You have been offered a position as a software developer, and you are keen to accept. However, the salary offered is about ten percent below the typical rate for the role in your city, and you have three years of relevant experience. The company has also mentioned that it could offer extra training or flexible working. The recruiting manager, Mrs Blake, has phoned you to ask for your decision. What would you say to Mrs Blake?
points: Express genuine enthusiasm for the role first
Give a reasoned case for a higher salary
Name a figure or a range rather than a vague request
Show willingness to consider the other benefits as part of a package

items.title: Proposing new scheduling software
items.situation: Your department still plans all staff shifts with paper forms and a shared spreadsheet, which often leads to double bookings and missing information. You have tried a free trial of an online scheduling tool and found that it saved you several hours a week. At today's team meeting, your department head has given you two minutes to make the case for adopting it across the whole team. What would you say to the team?
points: Describe the current problem in concrete terms
Give evidence from your own trial
Anticipate concerns such as cost or learning time
Suggest a low-risk next step, such as a one-month pilot

items.title: A client queries an invoice
items.situation: You work for a small design agency. A client, Mr Lawson, has phoned you, sounding annoyed. He says he agreed to pay a fixed price of two thousand pounds for a new logo, but your invoice is for two thousand eight hundred. You check the file and see that the extra charge is for three additional rounds of changes he requested, which were not included in the original agreement. What would you say to Mr Lawson?
points: Acknowledge his concern and stay courteous
Explain clearly what the extra charge covers
Refer to the original agreement without sounding defensive
Offer to send a breakdown or discuss options

items.title: Training a new intern
items.situation: A new intern, Tom, has joined your team this week. This morning he sent a customer's personal details to the wrong email address, and when you mentioned it, he said the checking process your team uses seems slow and pointless. You know the process exists because the company could be fined heavily for a data breach. Tom is friendly and keen to learn. You have sat down with him over coffee. What would you say to Tom?
points: Keep it supportive rather than a telling-off
Explain why the checking process matters
Connect the rule to what happened this morning
Walk him through what to do next time

items.title: Reassuring a worried client
items.situation: You are a project manager at a building company. One of your clients, Mrs Osei, is having her kitchen renovated, and the work is running a week behind schedule because a supplier delivered the wrong tiles. She has phoned you in a worried state, saying she is hosting a family celebration in three weeks and fears the kitchen will not be ready. You are confident the work can be completed in time. What would you say to Mrs Osei?
points: Acknowledge her worry and apologise for the delay
Explain the cause briefly
Give a clear revised timeline
Explain the steps you are taking and offer regular updates
